source.title: Frequency Is Not Sensitivity Identifying Safety-Sensitive Experts in Sparse MoE LLM
source.citation: M. N. A. Siddiky et al., 2026
source.authors: M. N. A. Siddiky; Liuwan Zhu; Yi Dong

page_placements.theme: Sparse components carry refusal: neurons, weight rows, attention-head groups, SAE/transcoder features, MoE experts

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present and readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests suppression of routed MoE experts, not the residual-stream direction or any of the specific claim versions. It cites the single-direction work as related motivation but does not rely on that direction as a method.
record.gate_note: The study reports refusal outcomes after suppressing gradient-, activation-, or randomly selected experts. These results concern expert suppression, not ablation or addition of the claimed residual-stream direction, a weight edit of that direction, or the other specified versions. I record the reported expert-suppression outcomes as findings that fit no version. The routing-concentration measurements do not measure the claimed direction.
record.test_reason: The study ranks and suppresses routed MoE experts by router-gradient or activation signals. It never computes, ablates, adds or weight-edits a difference-in-means residual-stream direction, so none of V1–V8 is tested. Arditi et al. [21] appears only in related work, as evidence that dense-model refusal is low-dimensional. Expert suppression is a related but different intervention, so its refusal effects are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that activation frequency is not a reliable proxy for suppression effects, and that router-gradient sensitivity identifies experts whose suppression reduces refusal more than activation or random selection, including when per-layer counts are matched. They report that malicious prompts show greater routing concentration despite overlap with benign prompts. They call the concentration-gap link (ρ=0.90, p=0.083, n=5) exploratory, and leave capability preservation and non-monotonic budget effects open.
record.recipe_differences: The study ranks MoE experts using router-gate gradient sensitivity or activation dominance and suppresses them with a negative router-logit bias. It does not calculate or intervene on a residual-stream difference-in-means direction.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported effects vary by model and suppression budget. Gradient selection is not uniformly better than activation selection: Qwen3 is an exception at the smallest tested setting in both the same-count and traffic-target comparisons. Suppression budget effects are non-monotonic in some models.

fits_no_version.finding: Same-count protocol: suppressing router-gradient-ranked experts reduces refusals more than activation-ranked selection in 24/25 model–K conditions and more than the random mean in all 25. The exception is Qwen3 at K=10.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In instruction-tuned sparse MoE models, suppressing router-gradient-ranked experts reduces refusal on held-out malicious prompts more than activation-frequency or random selection.

fits_no_version.finding: At nominal 1–5% routing-traffic targets, gradient selection again beats activation in 24/25 conditions and the random mean in 25/25. The exception is Qwen3 at 1%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The gradient-selection advantage persists under matched nominal routing traffic.

fits_no_version.finding: With per-layer expert counts matched exactly, gradient beats activation in 23/25 conditions with 2 ties. At the largest budget, DeepSeek gives 28.05% vs 4.88% and OLMoE gives 73.53% vs −29.41%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The gradient advantage in expert suppression is not explained by layer placement alone.

fits_no_version.finding: In OLMoE, refusals fall from 34 to 9 of 100 with no degraded outputs. A benign audit found no restricted or degraded responses; general capability was not measured.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Suppressing a few routed experts can remove much of an MoE model's refusal without breaking generation; broader capability preservation is not established.

record.problems: Only five architectures are tested. The authors describe the cross-model association as exploratory and based on five models. The traffic-matched comparison is not an independent replication because gradient sets are reused. Per-condition refusal results are primarily presented in a figure, and general accuracy, instruction following, and capability preservation are not established.
record.rows_left_out: Routing-concentration and overlap results in Table II, and most individual refusal-reduction values shown only in Fig. 1, are not recorded because they do not measure the claimed direction or a specified version; the text does not provide their individual numerical values.

untested.parts: No difference-in-means direction is extracted. No directional ablation, activation addition or capability check after such an intervention.
No weight edit orthogonalizing a refusal direction.
No analysis of whether jailbreaks suppress the direction. No adversarial training against its ablation.
No test of multiple directions, affine or cone structure.
Harmfulness representation is not separated from the refusal decision.
No cross-language, cross-variant or base-to-instruct transfer.
No reasoning-mode tests; Qwen3 is run in non-thinking mode.

record.verdict_notes: No rows bear on any version, so no verdicts are given. Per-model results not in the rows: baseline refusal counts (Mixtral 58, Qwen1.5 94, DeepSeek 82, OLMoE 34, Qwen3 94); peak gradient reductions (DeepSeek 28.05%, Qwen3 21.28%, Qwen1.5 12.77%, Mixtral 15.52% at K=5); DeepSeek at the 5% traffic target (28.05% gradient, 9.76% activation, 5.61% random). These would matter only for an MoE expert-suppression claim, not for V1–V8. A researcher might link this work loosely to V4 or V7 as evidence that refusal is localized in MoE components, but the study makes no claim about directions.

versions.untested_parts: No difference-in-means residual-stream direction is found, ablated, or added; preservation of general capability after that intervention is not tested.
No weight edit that removes the claimed direction is tested.
The study does not test whether attacks suppress the claimed direction or whether training against its ablation improves robustness.
The study does not test whether refusal is represented by multiple directions, a cone, or a dominant direction plus others.
The study does not separately measure harmfulness judgments and refusal decisions.
No cross-language, cross-variant, or base-to-instruct transfer of the claimed direction is tested.
The study does not vary refusal training or test when a removable direction forms.
The study does not test reasoning models or the claimed direction in them.

relation.reason: Arditi et al. [21] is cited once in Related Work, as dense-model evidence of low-dimensional refusal mechanisms. It is not discussed further or used.

tranche.reason: The study ranks and suppresses routed MoE experts (negative router-logit bias) using router-gradient or activation-dominance scores. It never computes, ablates, adds or weight-edits a residual-stream refusal direction, and it does not use one as a tool. None of V1–V8 is tested.

source_check.notes: The study suppresses MoE experts, not a residual-stream direction. Responses were labeled manually (number of labelers not stated). Qwen3 ran in non-thinking mode. General capability was not measured (the authors say so). The 'no degraded outputs' claim covers all three experiments. Same-count activation and random values appear only in Fig. 1, apart from Qwen3 K=10. Gradient sets are shared between the same-count and traffic-target protocols, so the 34 to 9 result is the same run in both.
